script.text: A clock inside an atom's nucleus just ran for a full day. Why care?

In a study published in Nature on October seventh, physicists in Vienna reported a working nuclear clock. A laser excites the nucleus of thorium two twenty nine, held in a calcium fluoride crystal about a millimetre across. Nuclei are far less disturbed by stray fields.

The team from TU Wien and Germany's national metrology institute P.T.B. says a feedback loop corrects the laser on its own. The clock ran unattended for more than twenty four hours. Its stability approached one part in a quadrillion over a day.

The catch: it does not beat today's best optical clocks. The researchers present it as a feasibility milestone. A team in China reported a second nuclear clock. The long-term hope is to test whether nature's constants change.
Will nuclear clocks one day redefine the second? Yes or no?

upload.title: Vienna Lab Runs a Nuclear Clock for 24 Hours #shorts
upload.description:
Physicists at TU Wien and Germany's PTB report a thorium-229 nuclear clock that corrected its own laser and ran unattended for more than 24 hours, according to a study published in Nature on October 7, 2026. It does not beat the best optical clocks; the authors present it as a feasibility milestone. A second nuclear clock from a team in China was also reported (from secondary coverage).

Sources: Nature (Oct 7, 2026); TU Wien / PTB press release via EurekAlert; Interesting Engineering; ScienceDaily.
